title: Identity-based encryption from arbitrary public-key encryption
formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply an adaptively IND-ID-CPA-secure identity-based bit-encryption scheme for identity space \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) with polynomial-size public parameters, under the classical standard-model conventions below?
definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u :N	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, Pr[Dec(\(sk,Enc(pk,b)\))≠b]\(\le 
u (\lambda )\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require |\(\Pr [ eta ' = eta ]- 1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. An identity-based scheme has \(Setup(1^{\lambda})\)=(mpk,msk), Extract(msk,id)=\(sk_{id}\) for every \(id\in \{0,1\}^{\lambda}\), EncID(mpk,id,b)=c, and \(DecID(sk_{id},c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). Public parameters include the scheme description, and mpk,msk,\(sk_{id}\) and ciphertexts have length bounded by fixed polynomials in \(\lambda\). For all \(\lambda ,id,b\) require Pr[DecID(Extract(msk,id),EncID(mpk,id,b))≠b]\(\le 
u (\lambda )\) for one negligible \(
u\), including setup, extraction and encryption coins. In the adaptive security experiment the adversary first receives mpk. It may request keys for identities of its choice, each query answered by a fresh run of Extract. It then selects a challenge identity id* not previously queried, two message bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and retained state. The challenger samples an independent uniform bit \( eta\) and returns EncID(mpk,\(id*,b_{ eta}\)). Further adaptively chosen extraction queries are allowed for every identity except id*. Finally the adversary guesses \( eta\). Its absolute advantage over \(1/2\) must be negligible. The number and total length of queries are bounded by the adversary’s polynomial size. Illegal challenge or extraction queries abort the game with an independent fair guess, contributing zero advantage. There are no decryption queries; all public encryption calls can be performed by the adversary itself. The existence implication permits non-black-box constructions and provides no random oracle, extra setup or assumption beyond the stated PKE existence. The key generator is part of the IBE functionality, not an external assumption.

context_blocks.text: Identity-based encryption lets a single public setup support a large collection of recipient names. Deriving it from ordinary public-key encryption would resolve whether this form of key management needs additional hardness.

The source proves a sharp limitation in the generic-group model and discusses constructions that overcome earlier restrictions by leaving that model. It does not establish an impossibility for arbitrary constructions from public-key encryption. The size of the identity space distinguishes the target from a polynomial list of separately generated public keys.

why: Compare the assumptions needed for basic encryption and large-scale identity-based access control.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute this existence implication for the full exponential identity space and adaptive key-extraction experiment. Selective-identity security, a polynomial list of preassigned identities, or a generic-group/black-box separation alone does not settle the target.
